title: Yesterday I was at home
goal: Talk about the past, and deal with two things at once: past-tense verbs that change with the speaker's gender, and the little word *som* that must stand in second place.
bekal: form past-tense sentences for any subject, with the right gender ending
put *som/si/sme/ste* in the right place — second place, always

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Aký si mal víkend?
dialogs.intro: Monday morning in class. Eva and Budi swap stories about the weekend.

notes: **Bol som but bola som.** Budi is a man, so he says *bol som*; Eva is a woman, so she says *bola som*. Slovak past-tense verbs **always** follow the gender of the subject — including when the subject is you. Learners from languages without grammatical gender forget this for months.

**Som always comes second.** Notice how the word order shifts in the dialogue: *Bol som v Košiciach*, *Ja som bol doma*, *Konečne som ochutnal*, *Nič som nerobila*. Whatever stands first, *som* comes straight after it — never at the start, never at the end.
**The third person uses nothing.** *Bol som* (I), *bol si* (you), but just *bol* for "he". Slovak drops *je* here, because the *-l* ending already carries the gender.

**Nič som nerobila** — a double negative again, and notice how *som* slips in between *nič* and *nerobila*. Short words always go into the second slot, even if that splits something that feels like one unit.

**Chodil som po meste** — the preposition *po* + locative means "around", not "after". *Chodiť po meste* = to walk around town. The same preposition means "after" when followed by a time: *po obede* (after lunch).

grammars.title: The past tense — stem + l + som
body: The Slovak past tense has two parts: **a verb ending in *-l* that follows the gender of the subject**, plus **the present form of *byť*** to mark who the subject is. The third person leaves out the second part entirely.
after: **How to form it: drop the *-ť* from the dictionary form and add *-l*.** *Robiť → robil*. *Čítať → čítal*. *Bývať → býval*. *Hovoriť → hovoril*. *Pracovať → pracoval*. For most verbs, that's all you need to know.

**The plural is always *-li*, whatever the gender** — good news that saves you half the table. (Formal writing distinguishes *-li* and *-ly*, but they sound exactly the same and that rule is no longer part of modern Slovak.)
**For the negative, just add *ne-* to the *-l* word.** *Nerobil som*, *nebol som*, *nevidel som*. The word *som* doesn't get negated.

grammars.title: Second place — the law that governs all short words
body: Slovak short words — *som, si, sme, ste*, *sa, si*, *mi, ti, mu, jej*, *ma, ťa, ho, ju* — are never stressed, and so they can never stand at the start of a sentence. They all gather in **second place**, right after the first part of the sentence.

head: Sentence
First place
Short word
English
rows: I was the one at home.

after: **The order inside the group is fixed:** *som/si/sme/ste* first, then *sa/si*, then the dative (*mi, ti, mu*), then the accusative (*ma, ťa, ho, ju*). This order never changes, and after a few weeks your ear will reject any other order before your brain can explain why.

**The most common mistake:** putting *som* at the start of the sentence (*Som bol doma* — wrong) or at the end (*Včera bol doma som* — wrong). If in doubt, ask: "what's the first word?" Then slip *som* in right after it.

**Why does the rule exist?** Because these words have no stress of their own, they have to lean on a word that does. Second place is where they can lean on the first word without breaking the rhythm. Czech, Polish, Serbian, and Ancient Greek do the same.

blocks.text: Most verbs just drop *-ť* and add *-l*. The nine below don't, and all of them are used every day — so learning them now is far cheaper than repeating the mistakes later.

Notice the pattern in the second column: **-šiel/-šla** for verbs of motion (*išiel, prišiel*), and **-ol/-la** for a few others (*mohol, jedol*). The masculine form slips in a vowel that disappears again in the feminine — *mohol* but *mohla*, *jedol* but *jedla*.

blocks.title: One tip that saves a lot of sentences
items: With irregular verbs, the feminine form is almost always **shorter** than the masculine: *mohol/mohla*, *jedol/jedla*, *išiel/išla*.
If you're a woman and unsure, try dropping the last vowel of the masculine form and adding *-a*. It's right far more often than not.

head: Questions and answers
English
rows: How was your weekend? (to a man)
How was your weekend? (to a woman)
It was my first time in …

blocks.text: Notice that **even the question follows the gender of the person you're talking to**: *Kde si bol?* to a man, *Kde si bola?* to a woman. You have to decide the form before the sentence comes out — which is why this part feels hard in the first week and stops feeling like anything by the third.
